summary_html: **Mandatory reporters** (designated professionals) must report suspected child abuse or neglect. Federal law sets the funding and policy floor (CAPTA) and mandates reporter frameworks on federal lands/facilities (VICAA).
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — federal floor for state reporting systems  
- **Victims of Child Abuse Act (34 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20307)** — includes federal-facility reporter duties (recodified from former 42 U.S.C. §13031)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The division held that the Child Protection Act and the Colorado Governmental Immunity Act can be read together, so that a public-employee mandatory reporter is immune from liability for reporting or failing to report child abuse unless the conduct was willful and wanton, and remanded for a Trinity hearing on that question.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling Colorado statement of the scope and limits of mandatory-reporter immunity under C.R.S. § 19-3-309, which is what makes the reporting duty at this node enforceable without exposing the reporter to suit.
key_cases.quote: persons who report child abuse under section 19-3-304 are immune from liability unless their conduct is willful, wanton, and malicious.

key_cases.case_name: Berges v. County Court of Douglas County
key_cases.holding: The division held that section 19-3-206's grant of exclusive authority to county attorneys over article 3 proceedings does not strip district attorneys of their authority to criminally prosecute mandatory reporters who willfully fail to report under section 19-3-304.
key_cases.relevance: This case establishes that a mandatory reporter's willful failure to report is a criminal misdemeanor prosecutable by the district attorney, which is the enforcement mechanism behind the reporting duty at this node.
key_cases.quote: section 19-3-304 does not set forth a proceeding under article 3; it simply defines an offense.

key_cases.case_name: Trinity Broadcasting of Denver, Inc. v. City of Westminster
key_cases.holding: The court reversed the summary judgment on the Governmental Immunity Act notice issue and remanded, holding that a pretrial governmental-immunity challenge is a jurisdictional question for the trial court under C.R.C.P. 12(b)(1), on which the court may permit limited discovery and must hold an evidentiary hearing when the jurisdictional facts are disputed, rather than resolving it on summary judgment or reserving it for the jury.
key_cases.relevance: This is the decision that supplies the procedure — the 'Trinity hearing' — a trial court must use to resolve a mandatory reporter's or agency employee's Governmental Immunity Act defence, which is exactly what L.J. v. Carricato ordered on remand.
key_cases.quote: When a public entity claims before trial that timely notice was not given to it under the Governmental Immunity Act, the trial court is the finder of fact.

key_cases.holding: The court reversed and remanded, holding that a public employee who asserts that his conduct was not willful and wanton under section 24-10-118(2)(a) is claiming sovereign immunity and may appeal its denial, that the trial court must resolve all issues bearing on that immunity claim including factual ones at a Trinity hearing rather than merely test the pleadings, and that willful and wanton conduct requires conscious disregard of the danger rather than negligence.
key_cases.relevance: It supplies the substantive standard and the procedure for the willful-and-wanton exception that strips a public-employee mandatory reporter of Governmental Immunity Act immunity under the rule stated in L.J. v. Carricato.
key_cases.quote: willful and wanton conduct is not merely negligent; instead, it must exhibit a conscious disregard for the danger.

mandatory_reporters: Enumerated professionals only — Colorado is not a universal-reporter state — Colo. Rev. Stat. § 19-3-304(2) (C.R.S. 2024); any other person may report voluntarily under § 19-3-304(3)
Physicians and surgeons, including physicians in training
Registered nurses and licensed practical nurses
Hospital personnel engaged in the admission, care, or treatment of patients
Public or private school officials and employees
Social workers and workers in any facility or agency licensed or certified by the state
Commercial film and photographic print processors
Clergy members (not for information learned in a communication privileged under Colo. Rev. Stat. § 13-90-107(1)(c))
Workers in the state department of human services
Officers and agents of the state bureau of animal protection, and animal control officers
Educators providing services through the federal WIC program
Directors, coaches, assistant coaches, and athletic program personnel employed by a private sports organization or program
Registered psychologist, marriage and family therapist, and licensed professional counselor candidates
Officials and employees of a county department of health or of human or social services
Employees of the department of early childhood
